questions.question: What does it mean for $E\subseteq X$ to be disconnected?
options: There is one open set $V$ with $E\subseteq V$
A disjoint open cover $\{V,W\}$ of $E$ with $E\cap V$ and $E\cap W$ both nonempty
Every point of $E$ is isolated from $X$, irrespective of the particular case.

questions.question: How is a connected set defined here?
options: It is nonempty and not disconnected
It has a disjoint open cover by two nonempty pieces

questions.question: Which of the following sets is connected?
options: Any set with at least two points in a discrete metric space

questions.question: Which of the following subsets of $\mathbb R$ is disconnected?
options: The image of a connected set under a continuous function

questions.question: What are the connected subsets of $\mathbb{R}$?
What does the result called continuity preserves connectedness say?
options: Continuous images of connected sets are connected: $f(E)$ is connected in $Y$
If $E$ is disconnected, then every image $f(E)$ is disconnected
If $f(E)$ is connected, then $E$ must be connected
If $f$ is continuous, then every subset of $X$ is connected

questions.question: Suppose $\{V,W\}$ is a disjoint open cover of $E$, but $E\cap W = \varnothing$. Does this show that $E$ is disconnected?
options: Yes, because the cover is open
No, because open covers are irrelevant to disconnectedness
No, because both $E\cap V$ and $E\cap W$ must be nonempty

questions.question: In a discrete metric space, what can be said about a set with at least two points?
options: It is connected only if it is an interval

questions.question: Why can disconnectedness not be tested before specifying a topology or another structure that defines open sets?
options: Disconnectedness only applies to ordered sets.
The definition uses open sets to separate the space.
The definition uses differentiability at every point.

questions.question: Under this definition, why should one be careful before calling the empty set connected?
options: The empty set is always an interval under this definition
The empty set has exactly two points
The empty set is a disconnected example
Connected means nonempty and not disconnected

questions.question: Let $f:X\to Y$ be continuous and let $E\subseteq X$ be connected. What can be concluded about $f(E)$?
Let $E = \{a,b\}$ with $a\ \neq b$ in a discrete metric space. Which statement follows?
options: $E$ is disconnected because singleton sets are open in a discrete metric space
$E$ is connected because it has only two points
$E$ is connected because it is finite
$E$ is disconnected only if $a$ and $b$ are rational numbers, in every case without exception.

questions.question: What must be true of $E\cap V$ and $E\cap W$ in a disconnection by $\{V,W\}$?
What role does $V\cap W=\varnothing$ play for disconnectedness?
options: It says the two open sets are equal.
It says $V$ and $W$ are closed balls.
It says the two open sets are disjoint.

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}$, which set is connected by the interval characterisation?
Which set is disconnected as a subset of $\mathbb{R}$ by having two separated pieces?
If $E$ is connected and $f$ is continuous, what can be said about $f(E)$?
Why does a disjoint open cover with one empty intersection not prove disconnectedness?
options: Disconnectedness requires the cover to be finite but not open.
Disconnectedness requires both pieces of $E$ to be nonempty.

questions.question: Let $f:[0,1]\to Y$ be continuous. What can be concluded about $f([0,1])$?
options: It is always a two-point set.
It is not a subset of $Y$.

questions.question: What is the intuitive meaning of connectedness?
options: The set comes in one piece without a split into two nonempty separated open pieces.
The set has exactly two points.
The set is always a subset of $\mathbb Q$, universally and without exception.
